extracted.intended_audience: authors (especially children's/YA authors) learning to write disability representation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on how to write disabled characters respectfully in children's and YA fiction and how to receive and respond to criticism about disability representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation in fiction can be incredibly empowering for disabled people and can shape non-disabled readers' perceptions, especially children and teenagers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should recognize the real-world effects of depiction: positive representations can normalize and empower, while harmful ones can perpetuate stereotypes and shape opinions. This makes striving for respectful representation worthwhile despite risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution, nuance, and context over checklist rules
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no single list of rules that automatically makes a portrayal right or wrong; what matters is execution, nuance, and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming a simple checklist will suffice; instead evaluate how a trope, trait, or scene is handled in the larger context of the work. A trope can be harmful or handled well depending on approach (fleshing out, deconstructing, lampshading, minimizing implications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disabled people are not a monolith
rubrics_metrics.description: Disabled readers have diverse experiences and preferences; not everyone will agree on what is or isn’t acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and respect differing disabled perspectives rather than seeking a single 'right' answer. Don't use one positive opinion as a shield against other critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small elements can perpetuate harmful narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: A single chapter, paragraph, or line can reinforce common, damaging narratives about disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should examine even minor elements for potential harmful implications, asking whether an element is essential and whether there is an alternative that preserves integrity while avoiding harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand history, context, and real-world effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism often points to historical patterns and wider social context that inform why certain portrayals hurt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When receiving critique, try to learn why disabled people might recoil: what message is sent, what history does it echo, and what are the real-world consequences. This deeper understanding is the goal of detailed critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen to multiple opinions and be willing to learn
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should genuinely listen to a range of disabled voices rather than becoming defensive or selectively choosing agreeable opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more authors listen instead of reacting defensively, the more they will grasp underlying roots of criticism. Listening includes accepting frustration expressed imperfectly (e.g., venting on Twitter) as valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dismiss critique based on tone alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism may be phrased unkindly or as venting, but that does not make it invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that marginalized people sometimes 'let off steam' after repeated hurt; consider the substance beneath the tone and avoid dismissing critiques solely because they are angry or snarky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cherry-picking convenient disabled voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not shield your choices by citing only disabled people who praise your work while ignoring those who object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage with the full range of feedback rather than using a single approving comment to invalidate others' concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be conscious and intentional in choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness of potential implications is crucial; struggling with a choice indicates consciousness and is a positive sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you find yourself worrying whether a scene or character choice is trope-y or harmful, that awareness means you want to do better—use it to refine the work rather than avoid the topic altogether.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tropes can be reused responsibly (fleshing out, deconstructing, lampshading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all tropes are automatically bad; they can be handled well if the author takes steps to minimize harmful implications or to critique/deconstruct them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider techniques such as fleshing out a stereotype, deconstructing it, or lampshading to avoid perpetuating harm. Evaluate whether the approach renders the trope harmless or reconstructs its meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of 'inspiration porn' and tokenizing portrayals
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayals that reduce disabled characters to inspirational objects or token traits are problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting achievements or framing disability in service of non-disabled characters' growth, question whether the depiction centers the disabled person's humanity and complexity rather than exploiting them for emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cherry-picking convenient traits or inaccurate portrayals
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting only 'convenient' aspects of a disability to fit the story can misrepresent experience and feel disingenuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for honest, complex portrayals rather than assembling agreeable traits that serve plot conveniences; consult and reflect lived experiences where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider whether disability is central or peripheral and the implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Deciding how prominent a character's disability is to the narrative affects reader perception—both ignoring it and making it the only defining trait carry risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh whether minimizing the disability sidelines experiences, and whether focusing on it reduces character complexity; aim for balance so disability is part of a full characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that criticism is part of the work of making literature safer
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversations and critiques about representation aim to make the literary world safer for marginalized readers, not to arbitrarily set hurdles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resent or fear those advocating for safer representation; their critiques come from experience of harm and a desire to change longstanding misrepresentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't be discouraged; improvement is possible and desirable
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing respectful disability representation is difficult and authors will make mistakes, but wanting to do better is a key part of progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors who are conscious and willing to learn are commended—persistence, listening, and revision can lead to success. The piece encourages authors not to stop writing about disability for fear of criticism.
